entries.question: Can a Bend proof kernel agree with the canonical AODL Python validator on pure structural policy checks, and does it give a latency benefit as a fast filter?
entries.finding: The CPU-only Bend kernel had 0 unexplained verdict disagreements with the canonical AODL validator on the frozen corpus. That is a correctness result only. The earlier CPU latency numbers do not cover the GPU path, and no GPU-path latency measurement of this gate has been published, so the latency question is open. Canonical AODL stays authoritative, and the gate is neither promoted nor rejected on latency.
entries.caveat: The parity result is self-reported in an issue correction with no raw output attached. It covers the CPU kernel on a single older machine, and the GPU path has not been measured for this gate.
entries.why: A fast structural filter is only safe to adopt if it matches the canonical validator, and it is only worth adopting if it is faster. Only the first of those two has been checked so far.

entries.title: does bend/hvm beat typescript for batch simulation?
entries.question: Does Bend/HVM give a meaningful throughput advantage over the TypeScript pure simulation core for realistic batch sizes, with semantically identical results on the same seed and tape?
entries.finding: Designed but not run: no results yet. The plan generates deterministic random and event tapes, runs identical workloads through the TypeScript pure core and a Bend/HVM batch runner, checks parity first, then compares warm vs cold, single vs multicore, and GPU only if the toolchain supports it cleanly. Kill criterion: if Bend/HVM shows no meaningful advantage after warm-up, or parity costs dominate, keep TypeScript and close the runtime experiment.
entries.caveat: Nothing has been measured; 'meaningful advantage' and 'realistic batch sizes' are not given numeric thresholds in the plan, and the work is blocked by an earlier task.
entries.why: It decides whether a parallel functional runtime is worth adding to a simulator, while keeping it out of the interactive 60 Hz path.

entries.title: a pure rules core must reach parity before any bend implementation
entries.question: Can the pickleball engine be split into a pure, sport-agnostic transition core that keeps parity with the green 2026 suite, with Bend limited to scoring and lifecycle laws and a second sport used as a falsifier?
entries.finding: Planned, not run: a seven-step ordered stack (#101 to #107) would freeze a verified 2026 pickleball rule profile, extract a pure transition seam without behavior change, and define a minimal SportRuleProfile. It would then add differential and property tests against the current engine, run a Bend laws spike and a badminton falsifier slice, and optionally benchmark Bend/HVM batch simulation. The stated baseline is 1,773 engine tests passed and 2,940 full-suite tests passed, with 12 skipped in each, and Bend implementation is explicitly forbidden until parity is shown.
entries.caveat: Nothing has been run. The baseline counts are self-reported test totals from the issue, and the design has no measured comparison yet.
entries.why: It sets a parity-first gate and a falsifier sport before committing to a new language for rules logic.

entries.title: can one camera with a movable split replace two viewers for evidence comparison?
entries.question: Can one synchronized camera with a movable split or wipe compare two spatial evidence states without opening two control stacks or dual Cesium viewers?
entries.finding: Design only, nothing has been run. The proposal compares imagery time A vs B, map source A vs B, radar/satellite time A vs B, and an annotated scene vs live state through one synchronized camera with a movable split or wipe, before considering dual viewers. Planned measurements are GPU cost, interaction clarity, and camera desynchronization.
entries.caveat: No measurement exists yet and no pass/fail thresholds or baseline are stated, so the single-camera approach is only a preference.
entries.why: If one camera works, evidence comparison needs less UI and GPU than two full viewers.

entries.title: does nanojev give a usable probability signal on abstentionbench
entries.question: Can the NanoJev backend produce a usable probability signal on one full RLCDAlignBench benchmark (abstentionbench, 150 rows), and if not, where does it fail?
entries.finding: Not yet run: this is a pilot plan. It asks for one run of the 150-row abstentionbench file through the NanoJev backend, reporting AUROC, F1 at 0.5, Brier, ECE, p50/p95 latency and failed-row count, with receipts for the code revision, checkpoint revision and input hash. It stops if the gated dataset or checkpoint is unavailable, if more than 20% of rows fail, or if the runner has a bug; a weak signal triggers inspection of state construction or backend semantics before more benchmarks.
entries.caveat: Design only, with no results, no baseline yet (direct Qwen/OpenJev comparison is a later step), and no numeric threshold defining 'usable'.
entries.why: It gives a cheap first real number and clear stop rules before investing in more integration code.

entries.title: can an external alignment benchmark test our detector probabilities?
entries.question: Can the gated RLCDAlignBench release serve as a licence-safe external battery for testing whether decision-backend probabilities are useful for detection, thresholding and escalation?
entries.finding: Not run. The design adds a benchmark-only external lane covering 7,193 labelled instances across 44 benchmarks and 10 failure families, scored with AUROC, F1 at 0.5, F1 under a fitted threshold, Brier/ECE and risk/coverage. The generic detector-metrics slice has landed, and the next gate is a 20-row pilot from one benchmark through a small local model. The full battery is only built if that pilot shows signal.
entries.caveat: Nothing has been measured yet: the numbers describe the benchmark's size, not any result, and the 20-row pilot is too small to say more than whether there is any signal at all.
entries.why: The project lacks external gold tasks and an operational calibration target, so this tests whether its probabilities can be trusted for thresholding.

entries.title: can desktop, tui and web share one attention state without a second status store?
entries.question: Can Hermes Desktop, TUI, and Web share one attention and voice-intent semantic without adding a second status store?
entries.finding: This is a design, not a result. The plan allows a maximum of 3 active experiments, each starting from a concrete user failure, an invariant, and a falsifying control. Wave 1 covers attention state, voice intent and pane intent. Every item is unchecked, and work is split into follow-up issues #14, #15 and #16.
entries.caveat: Nothing has been run. No experiment results exist, and upstream changes are switched off until receipts exist.
entries.why: It sets the pass/fail discipline for human-agent coordination UX before any code is changed upstream.

entries.title: does the list_apps cache remove the latency concern?
entries.question: Does upstream trycua/cua#3492 (installed-app scan memoization) fully absorb the remaining list_apps latency concern in trycua/cua#4055, so that a running-only enumeration option can be de-scoped?
entries.finding: Not yet measured. The planned test is a same-machine, exact-head Rust A/B of current main against #3492 on macOS: cold miss and warm hit, with 1 and 8 concurrent callers, reporting p50/p95 and scan count, plus install/uninstall invalidation and live running-app correctness. The decision rule is that if warm and concurrent behavior removes the practical critical-path cost and running-app results stay live, the running-only option is de-scoped; otherwise cold discovery for running-only callers becomes a separate measured requirement.
entries.caveat: No macOS run has happened; only Linux source review was possible, and Linux timing is explicitly not accepted as evidence for this question.
entries.why: It decides whether a new public API option is needed or an existing cache already covers the latency problem.

entries.title: do browser and gui routes really save time once every cost is counted?
entries.question: Do browser and GUI routes save elapsed time once every phase, failure, fallback and retry is counted against independently verified outcomes?
entries.finding: This is a round-2 measurement plan with five P0 experiments: a causal A/B of cursor feedback, a real CDP event wake, a real-provider guarded completion with at least 30 AB/BA-interleaved pairs, route diagnostics, and acknowledgement-loss faults. P1 adds compiled-routine accounting with at least 20 warm attempts per arm, plus matched-surface comparisons. A latency claim needs named spans to explain more than 90% of verified outcome time. All attempts must be kept, with denominators and paired uncertainty, and cold and warm timings kept apart. Earlier simulated and fixture numbers, such as medians of 7.459 → 7.718 ms and 102.628 → 16.580 ms, are cited only as motivation and are not expected production savings.
entries.caveat: This entry is the design, not a result. Later comments in the issue report some executed lanes, and each is from a single run with no transfer across sources, providers or machines.
entries.why: Counting only the successful fast path can make a route look faster than it is once failures and retries are included.

entries.title: does a guarded second action cut provider decisions?
entries.question: Can a caller-side guarded continuation admit a second action from a fresh post-mutation target, cutting provider decisions and task time with no success regression and no unauthorized second dispatch?
entries.finding: On a type-then-submit fixture in an isolated real browser session, the guarded arm used 1 provider call against 2 for the baseline, and both arms were verified as submitted by an independent oracle. Wall time to the verified submit was 1073.78 ms guarded against 1129.91 ms baseline, a marginal gain. An earlier run had stopped at a submit-ref mismatch because the ref is re-minted after typing. Binding the second click to the ref resolved from the post-mutation snapshot fixed that. Every negative control (refuted, unknown, stale, rebound, refused, missing capture, missing observation, old-ref reuse) had second_dispatch 0.
entries.caveat: One fixture run once on one machine. The wall-time difference is small and could be noise. Multi-task batteries and replay of may-have-landed actions were not covered.
entries.why: Skipping a model call between two predictable steps saves cost and latency, but only if it never fires a stale or unauthorized second action.

entries.title: does one executable candidate justify skipping the chooser?
entries.question: Does skipping the provider when exactly one executable candidate exists speed up verified UI actions without removing the chooser's abstention or reobserve option?
entries.finding: In 12/12 verified normal trials the fast path made 0 provider calls versus 12 for baseline, but median verified-outcome latency was 371.26 ms versus 346.66 ms, so no latency benefit was shown. In forced trial 999, with one executable candidate, the baseline chose reobserve (3 provider calls) and verified, while the generic fast path skipped the provider, acted immediately and also verified, so it removed a valid abstention that final success hid. The generic rule was rejected; a narrower rule (skip only when a bound completion id names the single candidate as the required completion of a locally proven obligation) was adopted but not yet measured.
entries.caveat: Mock provider time is negligible, so the latency comparison says nothing about a real model provider; only 12 normal trials and one authority counterexample on a single hosted runner, and the narrow rule is untested live.
entries.why: Success of the final outcome can mask a lost option to abstain or reobserve, so routing shortcuts need an authority check, not just an outcome check.

entries.title: does screenshot-only verification skip the accessibility walk?
entries.question: When verify_state takes its final screenshot read with include_screenshot:true, does it skip the accessibility-tree walk without changing screenshot output?
entries.finding: On macOS with Calculator, at the exact pull-request head, element plus screenshot verification dropped from 2 accessibility walks to 1. Window-only plus screenshot went from 1 to 0, and the element-only control with no screenshot stayed at 1. Screenshot dimensions and encoded size were unchanged.
entries.caveat: Only macOS with one app was measured, and the counts were reported in an upstream comment by an outside tracer. The Linux and Windows walker counts were never measured, and the requested trace logs are not stored in the repo.
entries.why: Skipping a needless accessibility-tree walk on every screenshot-evidence read could cut verification cost, but only if each platform honors the selector.

entries.title: does skipping observation recaptures pass a false-reuse gate?
entries.question: Can revision-aware conditional observation skip recaptures safely, with a skip rate and break-even measured from real invalidation traces?
entries.finding: A replay tool on synthetic traces produced a false reuse on a recorded GTK text change. Under the hard correctness gate, that kills the reuse policy that produced it. The synthetic skips were not treated as a real skip rate, so no real skip rate or break-even was measured. The simulator was closed, Phase 2B stays off, and always-observe is retained.
entries.caveat: Only synthetic traces were replayed, so there is no real skip rate, no break-even and no per-platform data. Real invalidation traces from the platform and browser census work are still missing.
entries.why: Skipping captures could save time, but one false reuse could authorize a wrong action. This shows the correctness gate matters more than the average skip rate.

entries.title: can typed action outcomes stop unsafe replays?
entries.question: Can a consumer use typed action outcomes (action effect, post-dispatch observation, refusal) to observe or stop instead of blindly replaying an action that may have already landed?
entries.finding: No measured run exists. The design compares a naive policy (retry when an action is unverifiable) against a typed policy (skipped or unavailable observation means observe before replay, refusal means stop) on a Calculator-shaped fixture. Planned metrics are duplicate harmful mutations, extra observations, task success and false completion. Comments state no fixture was driven; the policy is only encoded, and the runtime proof was moved to a separate live failure-injection issue.
entries.caveat: Nothing was measured: the typed policy behavior is encoded but never run against a fixture, so there are no results for either policy.
entries.why: Blind replay of an action that may have already landed can duplicate harmful mutations, so knowing whether typed outcomes prevent that shapes how agents handle uncertain actions.

entries.title: does a learned observe-vs-act selector beat deterministic gates?
entries.question: Does a learned risk/coverage selector over ACT / OBSERVE_MORE / ESCALATE add value beyond deterministic gates plus unconditional escalation?
entries.finding: Designed but not run. The plan is a shadow-only learned selector over a bounded legal action set, compared against a deterministic rule baseline, lexical/metadata routing, a simple ranking or logistic model, and a frontier teacher, using grouped held-out splits by project and work lineage. It would be scored on verified transition success and on system cost such as tokens, latency and frontier calls avoided, and no results exist yet.
entries.caveat: Nothing has been measured. The experiment waits on a frozen State Packet cohort, and teacher agreement is explicitly not ground truth, so outcomes must be joined independently.
entries.why: If a small learned selector cannot beat plain rules plus escalation, expensive frontier-model calls cannot be safely cut this way.

entries.title: can bend prove a few aodl compiler invariants?
entries.question: Can Bend laws and affine types express a few AODL compilation invariants without moving parsing, effects, persistence, or runtime into Bend?
entries.finding: This is a design only, with nothing implemented or measured. It proposes a small opt-in Bend proof kernel on a feature branch, with six targets: no invented authority, gate witness preservation, fail-closed lowering, determinism, intent immutability and affine capability semantics. A 2026-09-29 status refresh says default-branch code has no Bend integration, and a comment sets a kill criterion: keep Bend experimental if parsing, effects or runtime must move into Bend, or if the proofs add nothing beyond the existing fail-closed fixtures.
entries.caveat: Nothing has been built or run, so there is no evidence yet that Bend can express these invariants or that the proofs add value over the existing fixtures. The success criteria are only planned.
entries.why: It tests whether machine-checked proofs can strengthen a compiler's safety guarantees while keeping effects and authority under host control.

entries.title: can a/b tests validate research findings before integration?
entries.question: Can research findings be validated against real user data with cohort A/B tests before they are integrated?
entries.finding: This is a design for an A/B testing framework with cohort assignment (50/50 split), experiment configuration, intervention tracking, significance testing (p-value, effect size), and automatic halting of harmful experiments. All deliverables are unchecked, and no experiment has been run or measured.
entries.caveat: Planning issue only: no code, data or results exist, so nothing about effectiveness is known.
entries.why: A validation gate would show whether research ideas help real users before they ship.
